summary: This document presents a framework for interconnecting Content Distribution Networks. It gives an overall picture of the problem space and describes how the components relate, covering interfaces and mechanisms for things like request routing, distribution metadata exchange and logging.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7336 maps out how one content delivery network can hand requests and related work to another. It names five interfaces for setup, delivery areas, request routing, content rules, and logs. It describes a framework, not detailed protocols for those interfaces.

subtitle: A framework for passing requests, metadata, and delivery work between CDNs.

tldr.problem: A Content Distribution Network (CDN) may not cover every location or have enough capacity for every request. Interconnected CDNs need ways to route requests, exchange delivery rules, acquire content, and share logs.
tldr.mechanism: The framework distinguishes an Upstream CDN from a Downstream CDN and describes five interfaces: Control, Footprint and Capabilities Advertisement, Request Routing Redirection, Metadata, and Logging. It explains how those pieces fit together but leaves their detailed specifications to other documents.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7336 is an Informational framework. Together with RFC 6707, it obsoletes RFC 3466.

today: RFC 7336 is Informational. Together with RFC 6707, it obsoletes RFC 3466; the unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or obsoletes RFC 7336.

sections.title: The CDNI Framework
sections.content:
Content Distribution Network Interconnection (CDNI) lets separate CDNs cooperate to deliver content. The Upstream CDN (uCDN) has the relationship with the content provider; it can redirect a user's request to a Downstream CDN (dCDN), which may deliver the content.

This document expands on the CDNI problem statement and use cases. Its message-flow examples illustrate possible operation rather than prescribe a single implementation, and detailed interface specifications are left to other documents.
sections.plainLanguage: One CDN can direct a request to another CDN that can deliver the content. This RFC explains the roles and interfaces those CDNs need to coordinate.

sections.title: The Five CDNI Interfaces
sections.content:
The framework names five interfaces. The Control interface bootstraps the others and can trigger content or metadata pre-positioning and purging. The Footprint and Capabilities Advertisement interface shares information about where a CDN can deliver and what it can do.

The Request Routing Redirection interface selects a CDN or delivery node for a request. The Metadata interface carries rules such as geographic restrictions and availability windows. The Logging interface exchanges delivery activity for monitoring, analysis, or billing.

A successful Control operation means the requested action has completed. A successful Metadata exchange confirms receipt, but the metadata may take effect later.
sections.plainLanguage: The interfaces cover setup, delivery capability, request routing, delivery rules, and activity records. A successful control action means it is done; received metadata may take effect later.

sections.title: Two Ways to Redirect a Request
sections.content:
DNS redirection returns an address or a CNAME for the requested name. It is transparent to the user and can be cached, but the authoritative server sees the resolver's address rather than necessarily seeing the user's address. A resolver that ignores the DNS time-to-live can also bypass the Upstream CDN on later requests.

HTTP redirection returns a response such as 302 or 307 with a new URL. The CDN sees the user's HTTP request and can consider request details, but redirection is not cached and changing domains can affect application behavior, including whether a browser sends cookies.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS sends a name lookup to a different address, while HTTP tells the user's client to fetch a new URL. DNS can be cached; HTTP exposes more request details but sends each redirect through the CDN.

sections.title: A Request Through Two CDNs
sections.content:
Before requests arrive, a Downstream CDN can advertise its footprint and the Upstream CDN can pre-position metadata. When a request reaches the Upstream CDN, it may ask the Downstream CDN whether it can serve that request, then redirect the user.

The Downstream CDN serves a cached copy or acquires the content from the Upstream CDN. Later, the Upstream CDN can use the Control interface to request a purge, and the Downstream CDN can report delivery activity through the Logging interface. The framework also describes pre-positioning, synchronous metadata lookups, and multiple upstream CDNs.
sections.plainLanguage: The CDNs can exchange delivery information and rules before a user asks for content. The downstream partner then serves a cached copy or obtains one from upstream.

sections.title: Trust, Privacy, and Security
sections.content:
When a CDN delegates delivery, that downstream CDN may delegate again. The top-level CDN remains responsible for meeting the content provider's requirements, so the framework assumes peers will monitor each other and take corrective action when needed.

Interconnection can make it easier to share user activity data, especially through logs. The interface specifications must address privacy and confidentiality. Each interface must also operate securely over an insecure IP network, and peers must prevent their service from being used as an open proxy.
sections.plainLanguage: A CDN that delegates delivery remains responsible for its commitments and needs ways to check its partners. Logs can reveal user activity, so the interfaces need privacy and confidentiality protections.
